subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Edexcel spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Edexcel Sociology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: According to Murdock, which of the following is one of the four essential functions of the family?
questions.explain: Murdock identified four functions: sexual, reproductive, economic and educational (socialisation).

questions.q: George Murdock studied 250 societies and argued that the family is...
options: A source of oppression for women
questions.explain: Murdock (functionalist) claimed the family is universal because it performs four essential functions.

questions.q: Teaching children the norms and values of society within the family is which function?
questions.explain: Primary socialisation is the family's role in teaching children society's norms and values.

questions.q: Talcott Parsons argued the modern nuclear family has two 'irreducible functions'. These are...
options: Primary socialisation of children and stabilisation of adult personalities
questions.explain: Parsons identified two basic functions: primary socialisation of children and the stabilisation of adult personalities (the 'warm bath' theory).

questions.q: A household consisting of two parents and their dependent children is a...
questions.explain: A nuclear family is two generations: parents and their dependent children.

questions.q: A family where grandparents, parents and children live together or nearby is an example of a...
questions.explain: An extended family includes relatives beyond the nuclear unit, such as grandparents, aunts or uncles.

questions.q: A reconstituted (blended) family is one where...
options: Two adults form a family bringing children from previous relationships
questions.explain: A reconstituted or step-family is formed when partners bring children from previous relationships together.

questions.q: The Rapoports argued that family life in Britain is characterised by...
options: Increasing family diversity (e.g. cultural, organisational, life-course)
The decline of all family forms
A return to the extended family
questions.explain: The Rapoports identified several types of family diversity, arguing there is no single 'normal' family.

questions.q: Which legal change is often cited as a reason for the rise in divorce rates after 1969?
options: The Divorce Reform Act (making divorce easier/cheaper)
questions.explain: The 1969 Divorce Reform Act made divorce easier and cheaper, contributing to rising divorce rates.

questions.q: 'Secularisation' is used to explain rising divorce because...
options: Religion has less influence, so marriage is seen as less sacred
questions.explain: Secularisation (declining religious influence) means marriage is less often seen as a sacred, lifelong bond.

questions.q: 'Cohabitation' refers to...
options: A couple living together without being married
questions.explain: Cohabitation is when a couple live together in a relationship without being legally married.

questions.q: The rise in the average age of first marriage and more people cohabiting are examples of...
options: Changing patterns in family and relationships
questions.explain: These trends illustrate how patterns of marriage and family life have changed over recent decades.

questions.q: 'Segregated conjugal roles' describe a relationship where...
options: Partners share tasks and leisure equally
Partners have clearly separated roles and tasks (e.g. male breadwinner, female homemaker)
questions.explain: Segregated conjugal roles involve a clear division: separate tasks, responsibilities and leisure.

questions.q: A couple who both work and share housework and childcare equally have...
questions.explain: Joint conjugal roles involve partners sharing tasks and leisure, associated with Willmott and Young's 'symmetrical family'.

questions.q: Ann Oakley's research challenged the idea of the symmetrical family by arguing that...
options: Housework and childcare are still done mainly by women (the 'conventional family')
questions.explain: Oakley criticised Willmott and Young, arguing housework/childcare remains unequal and largely women's work.

questions.q: Oakley's concept of the 'conventional family' highlights that women often perform...
options: A 'dual burden' of paid work and unpaid domestic labour
questions.explain: Feminists like Oakley note women often face a dual burden or 'triple shift' of paid work, housework and emotional work.

questions.q: Feminist sociologists generally argue that the family...
options: Benefits men and can oppress women
Is equally beneficial to all members
Has no effect on gender roles
questions.explain: Feminists argue the family can reinforce patriarchy and disadvantage women, e.g. through unequal domestic labour.

questions.q: The idea that girls are socialised into domestic roles through toys and expectations is called...
questions.explain: Gender role socialisation teaches children behaviours seen as appropriate to their gender, including via 'canalisation'.

questions.q: A 'beanpole family' is one that is...
options: Long and thin: multiple generations but few children per generation
Wide, with many siblings and cousins
questions.explain: A beanpole family has several living generations but few members in each, linked to smaller family sizes.

questions.q: Which trend has increased the number of single-person households?
options: Rising divorce, later marriage and an ageing population
questions.explain: More divorce, later/less marriage and people living longer have all increased single-person households.
